subject: philosophy
title: Crito: obligation and justice
objective: Ask whether suffering injustice licenses doing it.

lesson.opening: TEXTUAL CONTEXT: Plato’s Crito presents Socrates in prison after his conviction. Crito urges escape. Socrates asks whether escape would be just, then the dialogue introduces an imagined speech by the Laws. Interpreting that speech and its relation to the Apology is contested.

sections.heading: Principle, application, and political obligation
sections.body:
The passage begins from a principle about wrongdoing and retaliation. Even if one has been wronged, it does not follow that doing wrong in return is permissible. That is not yet an argument that escape is wrong. A further application must connect escape to the prohibited wrongdoing.

The personified Laws later appeal to the city’s role in the citizen’s life, the damage of undermining judgments, and an alleged agreement expressed through remaining in the city. These are distinguishable grounds for obligation. Benefits, consent, and effects on institutions do not mean the same thing.

An objection may accept the principle against wrongdoing but deny that escape here violates a just obligation. Alternatively, it may challenge whether staying in a city constitutes genuine consent. These criticisms do not require endorsing revenge.

Do not flatten the dialogue into “always obey the state.” In the Apology, Socrates describes refusing unjust commands and imagines continuing philosophy despite an order to stop. Interpreters must consider how obedience, persuasion, justice, and particular civic obligations fit together. Your task is to expose that difficulty before resolving it.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: Reconstruction: One must not do wrong, even in response to wrong. If escaping in these circumstances would be doing wrong, one must not escape. The second premise carries the disputed application. The text’s later arguments try to supply it.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A serious objection accepts the ban on wrongdoing but argues that an unjust conviction need not create an obligation to remain. A reply must explain why this escape violates a genuine obligation, rather than simply restating the ban on wrongdoing.

activities.prompt: What principle is expressed in the excerpt?
choices: One should not return wrong for wrong.
Whatever is legal is always right.

activities.prompt: Which distinction matters in evaluating the Laws’ speech?
choices: Receiving benefits and freely consenting are not identical.
All obligations have one obvious source.
Remaining in a city proves assent to every possible command.

activities.prompt: A worker accepts that one should keep just agreements but denies that an exploitative contract binds them. What is disputed?
choices: The application or legitimacy of the agreement, not necessarily the general principle.

activities.prompt: Which reply actually addresses the unjust-conviction objection?
choices: Show why this particular escape would violate a genuine obligation despite the injustice.

activities.prompt: Does rejecting the application premise require endorsing retaliation?
choices: No: escape might be defended as not wrongful in this case.

activities.prompt: Why compare the Crito with the Apology?
choices: To assess whether an interpretation accounts for both obedience and resistance to unjust commands.
To decide which text has the nicer title.

activities.prompt: Reconstruct the argument against escape. Identify the premise you would challenge or defend, and give a reason.
activities.context: SOCRATES: Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him. But I would have you consider, Crito, whether you really mean what you are saying.
rubric: I state the principle and the disputed application separately.
I address whether this escape is unjust.
I do not equate understanding with agreeing, or law with justice without argument.
